items.readable_text:
Content:
For any two distinct points, there is always one (and only one) line that passes through them.

Content:
For example, the line passing through the points [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] is [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{PQ},] while the line that passes through [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5ff819ba753142463b69ef98546e7f5a]

Content:
However, given three or more points, there is not always a line that passes through all of them.

Content:
For example, for the three points [MATH: F, G,] and [MATH: H] below, it is impossible to draw a single straight line that passes through all of them.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b0489fa5c1ea83914c05a4ad71184361]

Content:
However, it is sometimes possible to draw a line through three (or more) points. In such cases, we say that the points are collinear.

Content:
For example, the points [MATH: M,] [MATH: N,] and [MATH: O] shown below are collinear since they all lie on the same line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c516f6af14be82b74e03f56ca93713ee]

sections.normalized_html:
Three (or more) points are collinear if a straight line passes through all points.

With that in mind, let's examine our diagrams in turn.

  • Diagram I shows three points that are not collinear. We can't draw a straight line that passes through all three points.

  • Diagram II shows three collinear points. There is a straight line that passes through all three of these points.

  • Diagram III shows three points that are not collinear. We can't draw a straight line that passes through all three points.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
For any two distinct points, there is always one (and only one) line that passes through them.

Content:
For example, the line passing through the points [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] is [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{PQ},] while the line that passes through [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5ff819ba753142463b69ef98546e7f5a]

Content:
However, given three or more points, there is not always a line that passes through all of them.

Content:
For example, for the three points [MATH: F, G,] and [MATH: H] below, it is impossible to draw a single straight line that passes through all of them.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b0489fa5c1ea83914c05a4ad71184361]

Content:
However, it is sometimes possible to draw a line through three (or more) points. In such cases, we say that the points are collinear.

Content:
For example, the points [MATH: M,] [MATH: N,] and [MATH: O] shown below are collinear since they all lie on the same line.
